To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

higher valuing, of the values Universalism and Security, predicted more positive attitudes and reduced consumption of each type of meat, while higher valuing of the value Power predicted less positive meat reduction attitudes and increased meat consumption.

(a) higher Universalism values are associated with more positive attitudes towards reduced consumption of meat, and lower frequency of meat consumption, (b) higher Power values are associated with less positive attitudes towards reduced meat consumption, and more frequent meat consumption, (c) higher Security values are associated with lower frequency of fish/seafood and white meat consumption, and (d) gender was not a moderator of the associations between values, attitudes and frequency of meat eating behaviour.

Universalism, Power and Security values were associated with attitudes and behaviour towards reduced consumption of red meat, fish/seafood and white meat, with Universalism being the strongest predictor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between personal values and attitudes and behaviour regarding meat consumption.
the role of personal values in meat consumption attitudes and behaviours.
the role of personal values as antecedents of meat consumption attitudes and behaviours, and the moderating role of gender in this relationship.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Universalism is associated with reduced meat eating behaviour, while Power is associated with increased meat eating behaviour, but that the effect of Security is dependent on the type of meat.
Universalism, Power and Security values influence attitudes towards meat reduced diet, which in turn influence frequency of meat consumption.
the higher one's Universalism, the more positive their attitudes towards reduced consumption of all meat types, and the lower their frequency of eating each meat type.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more a person values universalism, the more likely they are to eat a reduced meat diet.
the values people hold are associated with how they feel about meat consumption and how often they actually eat meat.
the more you value Universalism, the less meat you will eat.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people with high Universalism values are more likely to be interested in reducing meat consumption and to actually do so.
values, particularly Universalism, can be used to predict meat consumption behaviour, including the frequency with which individuals consume different types of meat.

people's meat eating attitudes and behaviour can be predicted by their values, and that the values that predict meat consumption behaviour are not the same as those that predict meat eating attitudes.
